    Atmospheric profile

    Both time sliders control the same hour.

    Now
    Snow level = wet-bulb zero height − 500 ft. The wet-bulb zero is where the wet-bulb temperature crosses 0 °C; melting and evaporation cool the air around falling snow, so snow survives below the dry 0 °C freezing level.
    DGZ = dendritic growth zone, the layer between −12 and −18 °C. Ice-saturated (RH w.r.t. ice ≥ 100%) air rising ≥ 10 cm/s through it produces dendrites and the highest snow/liquid ratios.
    Snow/liquid ratio (SLR) primary method: crystal-habit SLR of each ice-saturated layer, weighted by lift × thickness (Cobb & Waldstreicher 2005 style; thickness only for models without vertical velocity). No empirical wind or melting adjustment is applied until one is calibrated on multi-season data; an uncalibrated version is listed under Sources for comparison.

    Road conditions

    R-0
    No controls

    Dashboard shorthand, not a posted Caltrans level.

    R-1
    Chains, traction devices or snow tires

    Required on the drive axle of all vehicles except 4WD/AWD. Snow tires: M+S or mountain/snowflake, ≥ 6/32" tread.

    R-2
    Chains or traction devices

    Required on all vehicles except 4WD/AWD with snow tires on all four wheels. Exempt vehicles must carry chains.

    R-3
    Chains on all vehicles

    No exceptions. Rarely posted; the road is usually closed instead.

    CLOSED
    Closed

    Closed to traffic.

    Observations

    Measured, not forecast.

    Verification: past forecasts vs. snow sensors

    Each run's 48 h forecast at the sensor site is compared with the sensor's measured change once the window has passed. Snow-pillow SWE is the liquid reference. Sensor depth change is settled depth and understates new snowfall; the resort's new-snow boards are the better snowfall reference.

    Query points and elevation handling

    Ice-crystal habit vs. temperature and supersaturation

    After Nakaya (1954) and Libbrecht (2005). Temperature runs up the vertical axis like a thermometer. Dots: model levels at the selected hour that are ice-supersaturated, labeled in hPa.

    Supersaturation over ice is how much more water vapor the air holds than it would at equilibrium over a flat ice surface, in percent (RH with respect to ice − 100). Below 0 °C the equilibrium vapor pressure over ice is lower than over liquid water, so air that is exactly saturated for water droplets is already supersaturated for ice: about 10% at −10 °C and 21% at −20 °C (the dashed curve). Vapor then diffuses onto ice crystals and freezes onto them (deposition); the more vapor excess, the faster they grow and the more branched they become. In a mixed cloud the droplets evaporate while the crystals grow at their expense (the Wegener–Bergeron–Findeisen process). Temperature sets the basic shape (plates vs. columns); supersaturation sets how elaborate it gets, which is why big dendrites need both −12 to −18 °C and abundant vapor.
